prompt: The statement "Some laptops have a touchscreen" is about which part of the group?
optionA: Every laptop
optionB: At least one laptop, and possibly all of them
optionC: Exactly half the laptops
optionD: Most laptops but not all
correctAnswerText: At least one laptop, and possibly all of them
explanation: "Some" claims that at least one exists and stops there; it neither promises the rest do not nor fixes how many do. Reading it as "some but not all" adds a claim the statement never made.

prompt: The statement "All servers in this room are switched on" is about which part of the group?
optionA: Most of the servers in the room
optionB: At least one server in the room
optionC: The servers in the room and in every other room
optionD: Every server in the room, without exception
correctAnswerText: Every server in the room, without exception
explanation: "All" covers each member of the named group and no more. It is stronger than "some" and narrower than a claim about servers everywhere.

prompt: The statement "No tablet in the store has a keyboard" is about which part of the group?
optionA: Every tablet in the store, each of which lacks a keyboard
optionB: At least one tablet in the store lacks a keyboard
optionC: Most tablets in the store lack a keyboard
optionD: Tablets everywhere lack keyboards
correctAnswerText: Every tablet in the store, each of which lacks a keyboard
explanation: A "none" claim is as sweeping as an "all" claim, applied to the absence rather than the presence. Weakening it to "at least one" loses exactly what it asserts.

prompt: Which of these statements is the weakest — that is, claims the least?
optionA: All of the machines are new
optionB: None of the machines are new
optionC: Some of the machines are new
optionD: All but one of the machines are new
correctAnswerText: Some of the machines are new
explanation: A claim is weaker when fewer situations would make it false, and "some" is satisfied by a single new machine. Each of the others rules out many more possibilities.

prompt: A report says "Some of the tests failed". A reader concludes that some of the tests passed. Is that conclusion warranted?
optionA: Yes; "some" always means "some but not all"
optionB: No; "some failed" leaves open that all of them failed
optionC: Yes; a test that did not fail must have passed
optionD: No; nothing at all follows about the tests
correctAnswerText: No; "some failed" leaves open that all of them failed
explanation: The word "some" guarantees at least one and says nothing about the rest, so every test failing is consistent with it. Something does follow — at least one failure — so it is not true that nothing follows.

prompt: What exactly denies the claim "All the files were copied"?
optionA: No files were copied
optionB: Most of the files were not copied
optionC: All the files were deleted
optionD: At least one file was not copied
correctAnswerText: At least one file was not copied
explanation: To deny that every file was copied, one exception is enough. Claiming none were copied is far stronger than the denial requires, and would itself be a new claim needing its own support.

prompt: What exactly denies the claim "No student passed"?
optionA: At least one student passed
optionB: All students passed
optionC: Most students passed
optionD: Some students did not pass
correctAnswerText: At least one student passed
explanation: A "none" claim is denied by a single case to the contrary. Asserting that all passed overshoots the denial, and "some did not pass" is consistent with the original rather than opposed to it.

prompt: What exactly denies the claim "Some of the readings are above the limit"?
optionA: Some of the readings are below the limit
optionB: Not all of the readings are above the limit
optionC: No reading is above the limit
optionD: Most of the readings are below the limit
correctAnswerText: No reading is above the limit
explanation: Denying that at least one exists means asserting none do. The other options are all consistent with the original claim, so none of them contradicts it.

prompt: Someone claims "All the sensors are working". A colleague replies "That is false". What has the colleague committed themselves to?
optionA: That no sensor is working
optionB: That at least one sensor is not working
optionC: That most sensors are not working
optionD: That the sensors cannot be checked
correctAnswerText: That at least one sensor is not working
explanation: Calling a universal claim false commits you to one exception and nothing more. Taking on the stronger position — that none work — would need separate evidence, and is a common way an argument becomes harder to defend than it had to be.

prompt: Given only "Some programmers are designers", what is settled about the two groups?
optionA: They overlap completely
optionB: Some programmers are definitely not designers
optionC: The two groups have nothing else in common
optionD: They overlap at least partly; nothing more is settled
correctAnswerText: They overlap at least partly; nothing more is settled
explanation: The statement guarantees an overlap and fixes neither its size nor whether anything lies outside it. Every programmer being a designer is consistent with it, and so is almost none.

prompt: Given only "All tablets are devices", what is settled about the two groups?
optionA: Every tablet lies inside the group of devices; some devices may not be tablets
optionB: The two groups are the same group
optionC: Every device is a tablet
optionD: Some tablets lie outside the group of devices
correctAnswerText: Every tablet lies inside the group of devices; some devices may not be tablets
explanation: An "all" claim places one group entirely inside another and says nothing about what else the larger group holds. Reading it in both directions is what turns a valid statement into an invalid one.

prompt: Given only "No laptop in the batch is faulty", what is settled about the two groups?
optionA: They overlap partly
optionB: Every faulty item is something other than a laptop
optionC: The two groups do not overlap at all
optionD: The batch contains no laptops
correctAnswerText: The two groups do not overlap at all
explanation: A "none" statement is exactly a claim of no overlap between the two groups named. It says nothing about faulty items elsewhere, and it does not imply the batch is empty.

prompt: Students taking Python are A, B and C. Students taking C are B, C and D. Who takes both?
optionA: A and D
optionB: B and C
optionC: A, B, C and D
optionD: Only D
correctAnswerText: B and C
explanation: The overlap is exactly those appearing in both lists. Combining the lists gives everyone taking either subject, which is a different group.

prompt: All laptops are computers. This device is a laptop. What follows?
optionA: This device is not a computer
optionB: All computers are laptops
optionC: Nothing follows without knowing the make
optionD: This device is a computer
correctAnswerText: This device is a computer
explanation: Membership passes from the smaller group to the larger one, so the conclusion is immediate. Reading the first statement backwards gives a claim about all computers, which nothing here supports.

prompt: All prime numbers greater than 2 are odd. 13 is prime and greater than 2. What follows?
optionA: 13 is odd
optionB: All odd numbers are prime
optionC: 13 is even
optionD: 2 is odd
correctAnswerText: 13 is odd
explanation: The two statements combine to place 13 in the group of odd numbers. That all odd numbers are prime is a separate claim, plainly false, and it is what reversing the first statement would give — which is why it has to be rejected on its shape rather than on its content.

prompt: All sparrows are birds. All birds are animals. What follows about sparrows?
optionA: All animals are sparrows
optionB: Some sparrows are not animals
optionC: All sparrows are animals
optionD: Nothing, because three groups are involved
correctAnswerText: All sparrows are animals
explanation: Membership passes along a chain of "all" claims however long the chain is. Following it backwards gives a claim about animals that neither statement supports.

prompt: Some engineers are managers. All managers attend the review. What follows about engineers?
optionA: All engineers attend the review
optionB: Some engineers attend the review
optionC: No engineer attends the review
optionD: Nothing follows about engineers
correctAnswerText: Some engineers attend the review
explanation: The first statement puts at least one engineer among the managers, and every manager attends, so at least one engineer does. The chain carries "some" through as "some" — it does not strengthen it to "all", and it does not break.

prompt: The build fails whenever a test fails. A test has failed. What do the two statements jointly support?
optionA: A test has failed, which the first statement already told us
optionB: Every build failure is caused by a test failure
optionC: The build will pass once the test is fixed
optionD: The build has failed
correctAnswerText: The build has failed
explanation: The two together give the conclusion; neither alone does. Reading the first backwards would make every build failure a test failure, and the third option needs a further assumption about what else might break.

prompt: Every file in the archive is compressed. No compressed file can be edited directly. What do the two support about files in the archive?
optionA: No file in the archive can be edited directly
optionB: Some files in the archive can be edited directly
optionC: Every file that cannot be edited directly is in the archive
optionD: Nothing, since the two statements are about different properties
correctAnswerText: No file in the archive can be edited directly
explanation: The first places archive files inside the compressed group and the second excludes that whole group from being editable, so the exclusion reaches the archive. The properties differ, which is precisely what lets two statements chain.

prompt: All members have a card. Some cardholders are visitors. Someone concludes that some members are visitors. Both statements are true. Why does the conclusion not follow?
optionA: The first statement should have said "some members"
optionB: The second statement is about cards rather than people
optionC: The visitors who hold cards need not be the cardholders who are members
optionD: It does follow; two true statements cannot give a false conclusion
correctAnswerText: The visitors who hold cards need not be the cardholders who are members
explanation: Members are inside the cardholders, and visitors overlap the cardholders, but the two need not meet — the overlap could lie entirely among cardholders who are not members. True premises guarantee nothing when the step between them is invalid.

prompt: An argument runs: "Every experienced developer writes tests. Priya writes tests. So Priya is an experienced developer." Which step is not warranted?
optionA: Claiming that every experienced developer writes tests
optionB: Concluding that Priya is experienced from the fact that she writes tests
optionC: Claiming that Priya writes tests
optionD: No step is unwarranted; the conclusion holds
correctAnswerText: Concluding that Priya is experienced from the fact that she writes tests
explanation: The first statement puts experienced developers inside the test-writers, so a test-writer may sit outside that inner group. The conclusion is plausible and may well be true, which is what makes the shape of the step worth checking rather than the outcome.

prompt: An argument runs: "The three servers we checked were all patched. So every server in the estate is patched." Which step is not warranted?
optionA: Checking only three servers
optionB: Assuming a patched server stays patched
optionC: No step is unwarranted, since all three were patched
optionD: Generalising from three cases to the whole estate
correctAnswerText: Generalising from three cases to the whole estate
explanation: The observation is correct and the conclusion may be true; what is missing is any reason those three represent the rest. Checking few is a practical limitation rather than a logical error — the error is in what is concluded from it.

prompt: An argument runs: "If the cache is stale, the page shows old content. The page shows old content. So the cache is stale." The conclusion turned out to be correct. Which step is still not warranted?
optionA: Reasoning from the effect back to that cause, when other causes could produce the same effect
optionB: Claiming that a stale cache shows old content
optionC: Observing that the page shows old content
optionD: None; the conclusion being correct shows the reasoning was sound
correctAnswerText: Reasoning from the effect back to that cause, when other causes could produce the same effect
explanation: A conditional runs one way, so seeing the consequence leaves the antecedent open — the server might simply be serving old data. That the conclusion happened to be right does not repair the step, which is exactly why a correct answer is not evidence of correct reasoning.

prompt: If the server is down, the app cannot fetch new data. The server is down. What follows?
optionA: The app can definitely fetch new data
optionB: Nothing follows, because a conditional works only in the other direction
optionC: The app cannot fetch new data
optionD: The server must have been down because the app could not fetch
correctAnswerText: The app cannot fetch new data
explanation: Given the condition and the fact that it holds, the consequence follows directly. The last option reverses the conditional, which is the step that never follows.

prompt: If the licence has expired, the software refuses to start. The software started normally. What follows?
optionA: The licence has expired
optionB: The licence has not expired
optionC: Nothing follows about the licence
optionD: The licence will expire soon
correctAnswerText: The licence has not expired
explanation: Denying the consequence denies the antecedent, so a successful start rules the expiry out. This is the one direction other than the straightforward one in which a conditional does yield a conclusion.

prompt: If the disk is full, saving fails. Saving failed. A colleague concludes the disk is full, and the disk does turn out to be full. What follows from the two statements alone?
optionA: The disk is full, as the colleague concluded
optionB: The disk is not full
optionC: Saving will fail again next time
optionD: Nothing about the disk; saving could fail for other reasons
correctAnswerText: Nothing about the disk; saving could fail for other reasons
explanation: The conditional guarantees only that a full disk produces a failure, not that a failure requires one — permissions or a missing folder would do it too. The colleague turned out to be right, which changes nothing about whether the statements supported them.

prompt: Task B can start only after Task A finishes. Task C has no constraints. Which order is impossible?
optionA: B, A, C
optionB: A, B, C
optionC: C, A, B
optionD: A, C, B
correctAnswerText: B, A, C
explanation: The single constraint fixes only that A comes before B, and one of the four orders breaks it. C may sit anywhere, so its position never decides the answer.

prompt: A is to the left of B. B is to the left of C. What follows about A and C?
optionA: C is to the left of A
optionB: A and C are in the same position
optionC: A is to the left of C
optionD: Nothing follows about A and C
correctAnswerText: A is to the left of C
explanation: The relation carries along the chain, so being left of something left of C places A left of C. Two constraints that share a middle item are exactly what makes a third relation deducible.

prompt: Four talks run in some order. P is before Q. R is after Q. S is before P. Someone says the order cannot be determined. Which position is in fact fixed for S?
optionA: Second, because only P comes before it
optionB: First, because P, Q and R must all follow it
optionC: Last, because nothing constrains what follows it
optionD: It genuinely cannot be determined
correctAnswerText: First, because P, Q and R must all follow it
explanation: Chaining the constraints gives S before P before Q before R, which fixes the whole order and puts S at the front. "Cannot be determined" is the right answer to many such questions and the wrong one here, which is why the chain has to be followed rather than assumed incomplete.

prompt: Keyboard, Mouse, Monitor, Python. Python is the odd one out. What property separates it?
optionA: The other three are input devices
optionB: The other three are attached by cable
optionC: Python is the only one whose name is a word
optionD: The other three are physical devices; Python is software
correctAnswerText: The other three are physical devices; Python is software
explanation: Naming the property is what shows the grouping was understood. Calling the other three input devices fails, because a monitor is an output device — a rule has to fit every member of the group, not most of it.

prompt: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Linux. Linux is the odd one out. What property separates it?
optionA: The other three are programs for browsing the web; Linux manages the machine they run on
optionB: The other three are free to download and Linux is not
optionC: Linux is older than the other three
optionD: The other three run only on Windows
correctAnswerText: The other three are programs for browsing the web; Linux manages the machine they run on
explanation: The three browsers share a purpose, and Linux belongs to a different layer entirely. The other properties offered are either false or true of some members and not others, so none of them separates the group cleanly.

prompt: KB, MB, GB, GHz. Someone picks GHz as the odd one out, giving the reason that it is the only one whose letters are not in alphabetical sequence. Their answer is right and their reason is wrong. What is the property that actually separates it?
optionA: The other three are larger units than GHz
optionB: GHz is the only one used to describe processors
optionC: The other three measure amounts of stored data; GHz measures a frequency
optionD: The other three are abbreviations and GHz is not
correctAnswerText: The other three measure amounts of stored data; GHz measures a frequency
explanation: Reaching the right item by an accidental route leaves the grouping unexplained, and only the stated property survives being applied to every member. Units of data and units of frequency cannot be compared for size at all, which is why the first alternative is not merely wrong but meaningless.

prompt: A meeting must start after 2 pm and before 4 pm. Which proposed time satisfies both constraints?
optionA: 2 pm
optionB: 3 pm
optionC: 1 pm
optionD: 5 pm
correctAnswerText: 3 pm
explanation: The time has to be strictly later than 2 and strictly earlier than 4. Two o'clock itself fails the first constraint, which is where a boundary quietly slips past an inattentive check.

prompt: Constraints: the review is before the demo; the demo is before lunch; the retrospective is after lunch. A proposed schedule runs review, demo, retrospective, lunch. It satisfies two of the three constraints. Which one does it break?
optionA: The review must be before the demo, and here it is after
optionB: The demo must be before lunch, and here it is after
optionC: It breaks none; the schedule is valid
optionD: The retrospective must be after lunch, and here it is before
correctAnswerText: The retrospective must be after lunch, and here it is before
explanation: Checking each constraint against the proposal in turn is what settles it: the first two hold and only the third fails. Naming which constraint fails is a different task from noticing that something is wrong.

prompt: A rule states that scoring above 80 guarantees a distinction. A student scored 72 and received a distinction. Is that consistent with the rule?
optionA: Yes; scoring above 80 is enough for a distinction but need not be the only route to one
optionB: No; the rule means only scores above 80 receive a distinction
optionC: No; the score must have been recorded wrongly
optionD: Yes, but only if the rule was changed afterwards
correctAnswerText: Yes; scoring above 80 is enough for a distinction but need not be the only route to one
explanation: A guarantee makes a condition sufficient and says nothing about what else might also suffice. Reading it as the only route turns it into a requirement, which is a different and stronger claim.

prompt: Entry requires a pass in the entrance test. A candidate passed the test and was refused entry. Both the rule and the refusal are correct as stated. What does that show about the condition?
optionA: It is sufficient but not necessary; the refusal must have been a mistake
optionB: It is both necessary and sufficient, and the rule was misapplied
optionC: It is necessary but not sufficient; passing is required and something further is also demanded
optionD: It is neither, since the refusal contradicts the rule
correctAnswerText: It is necessary but not sufficient; passing is required and something further is also demanded
explanation: "Requires" makes the pass necessary, so nobody enters without it — and nothing in the word promises that a pass is enough. A refusal after a pass is therefore consistent with the rule rather than a contradiction of it.

prompt: An argument runs: "Our new page loads faster, so more visitors will complete a purchase." What does it assume without stating?
optionA: That the page loads faster than before
optionB: That load speed is among the things holding visitors back from purchasing
optionC: That visitors want to make purchases
optionD: That faster pages are generally preferred
correctAnswerText: That load speed is among the things holding visitors back from purchasing
explanation: The argument needs speed to be a cause of the outcome it predicts, and that link is never stated. The first option is a premise the argument does supply, and the others are true enough without being what the step depends on.

prompt: An argument runs: "Sales rose after we changed the packaging, so the packaging change worked." Every fact in it is correct. What must be assumed for the conclusion to follow?
optionA: That sales rose
optionB: That the packaging was changed
optionC: That packaging can influence buyers in general
optionD: That nothing else capable of raising sales changed at the same time
correctAnswerText: That nothing else capable of raising sales changed at the same time
explanation: Both facts are given and neither is in doubt; what carries the argument is the unstated claim that the packaging is what made the difference. That packaging can matter in general is not enough — it has to be what mattered here.

prompt: An argument runs: "Every complaint we received last month was about delivery, so delivery is our biggest problem." What does it assume, and how could you test that assumption?
optionA: That people complain about the problems that matter most; ask customers who did not complain
optionB: That complaints were received, which the argument states
optionC: That delivery can be improved, which is a separate question
optionD: That last month was typical, which more months would settle
correctAnswerText: That people complain about the problems that matter most; ask customers who did not complain
explanation: The argument moves from what was reported to what is worst, and that move needs complaints to be a fair sample of problems. People often abandon a service rather than complain, so the people who never complained are exactly where the assumption can be checked.

prompt: Two arguments reach the same conclusion. One states its assumption openly; the other leaves it unstated. Which is stronger, and why does the distinction matter?
optionA: The one stating its assumption, since stating something makes it true
optionB: The one leaving it unstated, since fewer claims are easier to defend
optionC: Neither is stronger in what it proves, but the stated one can be checked, and an unstated assumption cannot be argued against
optionD: They are identical, since both rest on the same assumption
correctAnswerText: Neither is stronger in what it proves, but the stated one can be checked, and an unstated assumption cannot be argued against
explanation: The logical content is the same either way, so neither proves more. What differs is whether a reader can locate the weak point — an argument whose assumption is buried survives scrutiny by being hard to examine rather than by being sound.

prompt: An argument assumes something that happens to be true. Does that make the argument sound?
optionA: Yes; an argument with true assumptions is sound
optionB: It removes one objection, but the argument is only sound if every step also follows
optionC: No; an argument that relies on an unstated assumption is never sound
optionD: Yes, provided the conclusion is also true
correctAnswerText: It removes one objection, but the argument is only sound if every step also follows
explanation: Soundness needs both true premises and valid steps, and a true assumption supplies only the first. An argument can rest on nothing but facts and still reason invalidly from them, and a true conclusion does not repair that either.

prompt: Evidence: of 200 users surveyed after a redesign, 150 said the site was easier to navigate. The survey covered users who had used both versions. Which conclusion is the strongest the evidence supports?
optionA: The new version is easier to navigate than the old one
optionB: Most users of the site find the new version easier
optionC: Some users answered the survey
optionD: Most of the surveyed users found the new version easier to navigate
correctAnswerText: Most of the surveyed users found the new version easier to navigate
explanation: The evidence is about the 200 people asked, and the strongest warranted claim stays with them. Extending it to all users assumes the sample represents them, and asserting the site is easier treats an opinion as a measurement. That some answered is true and far weaker than the evidence allows.

prompt: Evidence: every one of the twelve servers checked was running the latest version. Which is the strongest conclusion this supports?
optionA: All twelve servers checked were up to date
optionB: All servers in the estate are up to date
optionC: Most servers in the estate are up to date
optionD: At least one server is up to date
correctAnswerText: All twelve servers checked were up to date
explanation: The evidence covers the twelve examined and settles them completely. Any claim about the estate needs to know how those twelve were chosen, and "at least one" throws away almost everything the evidence gives.

prompt: Evidence: a fault appeared in every one of the five tests that used a large file, and in none of the twenty that used a small one. Which conclusion is strongest without overreaching?
optionA: Large files cause the fault
optionB: The fault has nothing to do with file size
optionC: File size is associated with the fault in these tests, and it is the obvious thing to investigate next
optionD: The fault will appear on any large file
correctAnswerText: File size is associated with the fault in these tests, and it is the obvious thing to investigate next
explanation: A clean split across twenty-five tests is strong evidence of an association and stops short of establishing a cause — something else may travel with file size. Naming the next step is exactly as far as the evidence reaches.

prompt: A conclusion is stated so cautiously that nobody disputes it and nobody acts on it. A stronger version would be acted on and goes slightly past the evidence. How should the strength be chosen?
optionA: By what will be acted on, since an unused conclusion helps nobody
optionB: By what the evidence supports, with the gap to the stronger claim named so others can decide whether to close it
optionC: By the most cautious version available, since caution is never wrong
optionD: By whichever the audience expects
correctAnswerText: By what the evidence supports, with the gap to the stronger claim named so others can decide whether to close it
explanation: Strength is not a matter of taste: a claim either outruns its evidence or it does not. Naming what further evidence would justify the stronger claim gives the audience a real choice, which quietly overstating does not.

prompt: Two conclusions are both supported by the same evidence. One is narrow and certain; the other is broad and probable. Is one of them wrong?
optionA: Yes; only the narrow one is genuinely supported
optionB: Yes; only the broad one is useful and therefore correct
optionC: No, but the broad one should never be stated
optionD: No; evidence can support claims of different reach, and which to use depends on what is being decided
correctAnswerText: No; evidence can support claims of different reach, and which to use depends on what is being decided
explanation: Support is not a single yes or no — a body of evidence backs a narrow claim firmly and a wider one less firmly, and both can be honestly stated if their standing is clear. What matters is that the reader knows which they are being given.

prompt: An argument runs: "Our tutorial works, because students who completed it scored higher than those who did not." The scores quoted are accurate. Which further fact most undermines it?
optionA: Students chose whether to complete the tutorial, and the more motivated ones did
optionB: A few students who completed it scored poorly
optionC: The tutorial took longer than expected to write
optionD: Another company's tutorial produced similar results
correctAnswerText: Students chose whether to complete the tutorial, and the more motivated ones did
explanation: The argument needs the two groups to be comparable, and self-selection breaks exactly that, leaving the scores intact but the inference broken. A handful of poor scores is consistent with the claim, and the other facts touch nothing the argument rests on.

prompt: An argument runs: "Response times improved after we added a second server, so the extra server is what did it." Which fact would most weaken it without contradicting the improvement?
optionA: Response times are still slower than a competitor's
optionB: The second server cost more than expected
optionC: Traffic fell sharply in the same week for unrelated reasons
optionD: Response times improved by less than the team hoped
correctAnswerText: Traffic fell sharply in the same week for unrelated reasons
explanation: Weakening means removing the reason to believe the link, not denying the outcome. A drop in traffic explains the improvement without the server, while the other facts leave the causal story untouched and merely make it less pleasing.

prompt: Someone attacks an argument by showing its conclusion is false. Someone else attacks it by showing an assumption is unwarranted. What is the difference in what each establishes?
optionA: They establish the same thing by different routes
optionB: The first shows the conclusion is wrong; the second shows the argument does not establish it, leaving the conclusion open
optionC: The first is weaker, since a conclusion can be false by accident
optionD: The second establishes that the conclusion is false
correctAnswerText: The first shows the conclusion is wrong; the second shows the argument does not establish it, leaving the conclusion open
explanation: An argument can be bad and its conclusion still true, which is why undermining the reasoning settles less than refuting the claim. Confusing the two leads to treating a defeated argument as a refuted position.

prompt: An argument rests on one assumption. A critic can either dispute that assumption or gather evidence against the conclusion. Which is the more efficient line of attack, and when does the other become necessary?
optionA: Gathering evidence, since evidence always outweighs argument
optionB: Disputing the assumption, since an argument with a disputed assumption is refuted
optionC: Neither; a single-assumption argument cannot be attacked
optionD: Disputing the assumption, since the whole argument depends on it; evidence against the conclusion is needed when the assumption turns out to hold
correctAnswerText: Disputing the assumption, since the whole argument depends on it; evidence against the conclusion is needed when the assumption turns out to hold
explanation: One assumption carrying an argument is its narrowest point, so pressing there costs least. But disputing an assumption only removes the support — if it holds after all, the conclusion is still standing and has to be met on its own terms.
